english.html: both places speaks very generally of all the well-born, and nevertheless speaks indefinitely of punishment <sup class="mk" data-key="ſ">ſ</sup>; and he who speaks universally of all comprehends all also, and excludes nothing <sup class="mk" data-key="t">t</sup>; and a proposition indefinitely pronounced weighs as much, and is of as great force, as the universal <sup class="mk" data-key="u">u</sup>. But what of it? In France we are outside this dispute, inasmuch as by the general custom of our Gaul the goods of one who is condemned to death — not only for the privileged crimes of lèse-majesté, heresy or false coining, but also for every other crime from which there follows natural death, mutilation of a limb or perpetual banishment — are confiscated, and the new constitution of Justinian has no place <sup class="mk" data-key="x">x</sup>; so that, as by a perpetual law, we say in France: WHO confiscates the body confiscates the goods <sup class="mk" data-key="y">y</sup>. And so the condemned man, being deprived of all his goods, could not make a testament <sup class="mk" data-key="z">z</sup>. By the first reason touched on above, one single case is admitted in which he who is condemned may make a testament: namely, when he is condemned by a judge not competent over him, as for example, and following the laws of our Pontiffs, if a clerk were condemned by a lay judge <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; in which case the condemned man does not lose the faculty of being able to make a testament, or otherwise to dispose <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>, inasmuch as all the procedure done by the judge is without any force, and as if not done <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>. And where there is want of jurisdiction and of power, the judgment never draws to itself the effect of the law <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>.
